short: The PLAG proteins - PLAG1, PLAGL1 (also called ZAC1 or LOT1) and PLAGL2 - are C2H2 zinc-finger factors with seven fingers that read a bipartite G-rich site: a GRGGC core and a GGG cluster separated by roughly six to eight base pairs. Finger 3 contacts the G-cluster and fingers 6 and 7 contact the core, so the two halves are read by different parts of one protein. PLAG1 is the classic translocation target in salivary-gland pleomorphic adenoma, where promoter swapping with CTNNB1 or LIFR switches it on; PLAGL2 is also transforming, while PLAGL1/ZAC1 is an imprinted, maternally silenced growth suppressor whose loss of imprinting causes transient neonatal diabetes. All three activate IGF2.
long:
## The factors

Three human genes make up this family. PLAG1 (8q12) was identified as the gene activated by promoter
swapping in pleomorphic adenomas of the salivary gland carrying t(3;8)(p21;q12), which fuses the CTNNB1
promoter to the PLAG1 coding region [PMID:9020842]; a second recurrent translocation, t(5;8)(p13;q12), puts PLAG1 under
the LIFR promoter. PLAGL1 (6q24), independently named ZAC1 for zinc finger with apoptosis and cell-cycle
arrest [PMID:9184226] and LOT1 for lost on transformation, and PLAGL2 (20q11) complete the set. All three carry seven
Cys2-His2 zinc fingers in a conserved N-terminal DNA-binding domain plus a C-terminal
serine/threonine/proline-rich transactivation domain, and all bind DNA as monomers. The DNA-binding
domains are highly similar in sequence [PMID:11888928], which is the central problem for interpreting a hit. PLAG1 and
PLAGL2 are broadly expressed in embryonic tissues and largely silenced after birth; PLAGL1 is expressed
from the paternal allele only [PMID:10655556], in pituitary, brain, pancreatic islets and many embryonic tissues.
PLAG1 activity is further tuned by SUMOylation of its transactivation domain.

## The motif

The literature consensus is bipartite: a GRGGC core and a G-cluster. The binding-site selection that
defined it placed seven random nucleotides between the core and a G-cluster written RGGK [PMID:10646861]; the
same group's later target-gene screen quoted it as GRGGC(N)6-8GGG, allowing six to eight [PMID:14712223]. How far
the spacer can vary has not been measured directly, but to the extent it does, the element is better described
as two half-sites than as a fixed-width matrix. Mutational and
binding work assigned the two halves to different fingers: finger 3 engages the G-cluster, fingers 6 and
7 engage the GRGGC core, so a single molecule bridges the gap [PMID:10646861].

The data in this atlas are consistent with that but compress it. The JASPAR PLAG1 model
(GGGGCCCAAGGGGG, 14 bp) and the equivalent CIS-BP and Vierstra models (CCCCCTTGGGCCCC) [PMID:25215497,32728250] span the whole
bipartite element with the short end of the spacer; the PLAGL2 and PLAGL models collapse to an 8-bp
GGGCCCCC, effectively just the G-rich halves. The atlas medoid, GGGCCCCC, is therefore shorter than the
literature consensus rather than in conflict with it: fixed-width position weight matrices cannot
represent a variable spacer, so the databases store the tightest-spaced version. Expect real sites to be
longer and more variably spaced than any of these matrices.

The three paralogues are not equivalent in vitro. PLAG1 and PLAGL2 bind the same bipartite site and both
transform NIH3T3 cells, whereas PLAGL1/ZAC1 binds a distinguishable, more homogeneously G-rich sequence
and arrests rather than promotes growth [PMID:11888928,9184226]. The CIS-BP PLAGL1 model here is a 4-bp CCCC inferred from mouse
Plagl1 at 88% DNA-binding-domain identity [PMID:25215497], so it carries almost no information and should not be used
for scanning.

## Where it acts

PLAG-family sites are G-rich and land preferentially in GC-rich, CpG-island promoters. The best-validated
target is IGF2: PLAG1 and PLAGL2 both bind the IGF2 P3 promoter region and up-regulate it, and IGF2
induction accompanies PLAG1- and PLAGL2-driven transformation [PMID:10646861,11888928]. PLAGL1/ZAC1 sits at the top of an
imprinted gene network that includes IGF2, H19, CDKN1C, DLK1 and MEST, and coordinates their expression
during embryonic growth [PMID:17084362]. Because the sites are G-rich, they overlap the binding preferences of KLF/SP
factors, EGR, MAZ, PATZ1 and other GC-box readers, and PLAG matches are common in the CpG-island
promoters of housekeeping genes where none of these factors is necessarily the functional occupant.

## Biology and disease

PLAG1 is the defining oncogene of salivary-gland pleomorphic adenoma [PMID:9020842] and also of lipoblastoma, where
the HAS2 or COL1A2 promoter is fused to the entire PLAG1 coding sequence, again a promoter swap rather than
a chimeric protein [PMID:10987300]. PLAGL2 is amplified and overexpressed in glioma and colorectal cancer and
promotes proliferation partly through WNT-dependent [PMID:20478531] and partly through IGF2/ASCL2-dependent routes [PMID:37310750].
PLAGL1/ZAC1 has the opposite behaviour: it induces apoptosis and G1 arrest [PMID:9184226], is imprinted with maternal
silencing [PMID:10655556], and relaxation of that imprint at the 6q24 HYMAI/PLAGL1 locus causes transient neonatal
diabetes mellitus [PMID:10655556,11448939]. Zac1-null mice are growth-restricted [PMID:17084362], consistent with a network role in embryonic
growth. Outside disease, a regulatory variant at the bovine PLAG1-CHCHD7 interval is one of the largest
single-locus effects on stature and carcass weight in cattle [PMID:22607022,29215042], a reminder that PLAG1 dosage controls
growth in normal physiology.

## Reading a hit

A PLAG match is a G-rich, GC-box-like element, so the honest conclusion from sequence alone is "a G-rich
promoter element," not "a PLAG site." KLF, SP, EGR, MAZ, PATZ1 and ZNF263 all compete for the same
matches, and G-rich matrices produce many chance hits in CpG islands. Within the family, PLAG1 and
PLAGL2 cannot be told apart by sequence; PLAGL1 is somewhat distinguishable in vitro, but the PLAGL1
matrices available here are too short (4-8 bp) to exploit that. Because the true element is bipartite,
with a spacer of about seven bases that later work quotes as six to eight, a fixed-width matrix will miss differently spaced real sites and may score
contiguous G-runs that are not functional sites. Check for the two halves explicitly if the call
matters. Expression is the strongest discriminator: PLAG1 and PLAGL2 are largely embryonic, so in adult
tissue a PLAG match is more likely to be a generic GC-box unless a fusion or amplification is known.
caveats: The real element is bipartite, a GRGGC core and a G-cluster seven bases apart in the original selection and quoted as six to eight in later work, and a fixed-width matrix represents only one spacing, so the matrices here are truncated or tightest-spaced versions that will both miss differently spaced sites and over-call plain G-runs. Matches overlap KLF/SP, EGR, MAZ and other GC-box factors, and G-rich models hit CpG-island promoters frequently by chance. PLAG1 and PLAGL2 share a specificity and cannot be separated by sequence; PLAGL1/ZAC1 differs in vitro, but its models here (CCCC, TGGGGCCA) are too short to use, and the CIS-BP PLAGL1 entry is inferred from mouse at 88% DBD identity. PLAG1 and PLAGL2 are largely embryonic, so adult-tissue matches deserve extra scepticism.

timeline.finding: PLAG1 is identified as the 8q12 gene activated in pleomorphic adenomas with t(3;8)(p21;q12), where promoter swapping with CTNNB1 drives expression of an intact PLAG1 coding sequence.
timeline.methods: Translocation breakpoint cloning; expression analysis of tumors
timeline.open: PLAG1 was a predicted zinc-finger protein with no known DNA-binding specificity.

timeline.finding: Zac1 (PLAGL1) is cloned as a zinc-finger protein that induces apoptosis and G1 arrest and suppresses tumor formation, the opposite of PLAG1's oncogenic behavior.
timeline.methods: cDNA cloning; proliferation, apoptosis and nude-mouse tumorigenicity assays

timeline.finding: The PLAG1 site is defined as a bipartite element, a GRGGC core and a G-cluster separated by seven random nucleotides, contacted by fingers 6-7 and finger 3 respectively; IGF2 promoter 3 is a bound and activated target.
timeline.methods: Binding-site selection; zinc-finger mutagenesis; gel shift; transactivation; tumor expression
timeline.open: Whether PLAGL1 and PLAGL2 read the same element was untested.

timeline.finding: ZAC/PLAGL1 is shown to be imprinted and paternally expressed at 6q24, making it the leading candidate for transient neonatal diabetes; loss of methylation at the HYMAI/ZAC imprinting control region is then found in most patients with a normal karyotype.
timeline.methods: Restriction landmark genome scanning; allele-specific RT-PCR; methylation analysis; reporter assays

timeline.finding: Despite highly homologous DNA-binding domains, the three PLAG proteins split in DNA binding: PLAG1 and PLAGL2 both need the GRGGC core and the G-cluster, with finger 3 reading the cluster, whereas PLAGL1 recognizes only an extended core; PLAG1 and PLAGL2 transform NIH3T3 cells and induce IGF2, in contrast to growth-suppressive PLAGL1.
timeline.methods: Transformation and nude-mouse assays; DNA-binding assays; expression analysis
timeline.open: Which residues give PLAGL1 its different preference was not identified.

timeline.finding: Zac1 knockout causes intrauterine growth restriction, and Zac1 is placed in a network of co-regulated imprinted growth genes, directly regulating Igf2/H19 through a shared enhancer.
timeline.methods: Knockout mice; microarray meta-analysis; binding and expression assays

timeline.finding: PLAGL2 is identified as an oncogene targeted by amplification or gain in malignant glioma, where it suppresses neural stem cell differentiation partly by modulating Wnt/beta-catenin signaling.
timeline.methods: Integrated copy-number and expression genomics; neural stem cell differentiation assays; transcriptome analysis

timeline.finding: In colorectal cancer, PLAGL2 drives transformation with only modest effects on canonical Wnt signaling, acting instead through direct targets IGF2 and ASCL2, which revises the Wnt-centered model for this tissue.
timeline.methods: Gain- and loss-of-function in CRC lines and intestinal cells; reporter assays; rescue with ASCL2
timeline.open: Whether the glioma and colorectal mechanisms differ by tissue or reflect a disagreement is unresolved.

open: The spacer is stated inconsistently: the original PLAG1 selection placed seven random nucleotides between the GRGGC core and the G-cluster, while the consensus usually quoted allows six to eight, and no genome-wide measurement has established how much spacer variation PLAG1 tolerates in vivo.

How PLAGL1 acquires a DNA preference different from PLAG1 and PLAGL2, despite a highly homologous DNA-binding domain, has not been explained structurally, and the PLAGL1 matrices in these databases (CCCC and TGGGGCCA) are too short to show the difference.

Whether PLAGL2's oncogenic activity runs through WNT signaling is disputed: in glioma and neural stem cells it was attributed in part to Wnt/beta-catenin modulation, whereas in colorectal cancer its effect on canonical WNT signaling was minimal and IGF2 and ASCL2 carried the effect.
